title: Five hazards of human spaceflight
summary: NASA groups spaceflight hazards into radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile closed environments. ASTRA uses those domains to organize a research simulation; the taxonomy is not a diagnostic model.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of NASA public material; no NASA endorsement.

title: Human spaceflight risks: sleep, cardiovascular adaptation and fitness
section: Physiology; Behavioral Performance and Human Factors
summary: NASA identifies inadequate sleep and irregular schedules, cardiovascular adaptation, immune changes, and reduced fitness among spaceflight research risks. Exercise is studied as a countermeasure to losses in bone, muscle and cardiovascular performance. These categories support longitudinal observation and human review, not diagnosis from a pulse or a brief reaction test.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA overview.

title: Exploration Medical Capability CDSS Architecture Recommendation
summary: The ExMC architecture links medical data management with decision support for missions where communication delay and resource constraints limit reliance on Earth. ASTRA borrows the separation of collected evidence and review support, without claiming to implement NASA's clinical capability or certification.
license_notes: Paraphrase of public abstract only. Full document may contain protected portions.

title: Earth Independent Medical Operations Datascope
section: Public abstract; input vectors and limitations
summary: EIMO considers combining wearable, behavioral, environmental, laboratory and record data with embedded reference resources. Its abstract also identifies insufficient representative training data and unreliable AI outputs as operational challenges. ASTRA therefore keeps deterministic monitoring separate from its constrained explanation workflow.
license_notes: Paraphrase of public abstract only; not a clinical protocol.

title: Exploration Electronic Health Record (xEHR)
summary: Exploration health records must support crew access and asynchronous sharing when distance prevents continuous ground support. ASTRA demonstrates that principle with local records, separate event and receipt timestamps, and a durable delayed-message queue. The simulated queue is not a deployed space communication system.
license_notes: Project-authored paraphrase of public NASA record.

title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1: Crew Health
section: Standard landing page; crew health scope
summary: Volume 1 is NASA's crew-health standard reference. ASTRA links to it for requirements context. This local research prototype has not been assessed for compliance and does not reproduce a treatment protocol.
license_notes: Landing-page metadata and scope, not a reproduced standard.

title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2: Human Factors, Habitability and Environmental Health
section: Standard landing page; environmental and interface scope
summary: Volume 2 covers human factors, habitability and environmental health. ASTRA presents cabin context and accessible interface controls as a simulation; its illustrative environmental warnings are not certified exposure limits.
license_notes: Landing-page scope, not copied requirements.

title: NASA Open Science Data Repository
summary: OSDR provides space life-science research data and associated context. Research datasets and processed laboratory measurements are distinct from a continuous crew medical feed. ASTRA links to public study catalogues; no personal NASA astronaut records are streamed into this demo.
license_notes: Overview paraphrase. Check each dataset's access and license separately.

title: BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset v1.0.0
summary: BIDMC contains 53 eight-minute recordings with ECG, PPG and respiration signals sampled at 125 Hz, alongside lower-rate numerics. These hospital recordings can test a signal pipeline, but they do not establish healthy astronaut baselines. The current ASTRA demo generates synthetic scalar readings; it has not downloaded or replayed these files.
license_notes: Dataset: Open Data Commons Attribution License v1.0; preserve authors' citation if acquired. Summary is a short paraphrase.

title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework 1.0
summary: NIST's AI RMF provides a framework to govern, map, measure and manage AI risks. ASTRA records model limitations, provenance and evaluation evidence; referring to the framework does not demonstrate medical validity.
license_notes: Project-authored paraphrase of a public US government publication.

title: NASA Human Research Program: the 17 human health risks
summary: NASA's Human Research Program tracks 17 human health risks in three groups: 11 physiology risks (immune, sensorimotor and vestibular, cardiovascular, decompression sickness, host-microorganism interactions, hypoxia, food and nutrition, spacewalk injury, cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness, SANS, bone changes), 5 behavioral and human-factors risks (behavioral conditions, teamwork, sleep and schedules, systems operations support, dynamic loads) and 1 radiation risk (radiation-induced cancers). How strongly each applies depends on whether a mission goes to low Earth orbit, the Moon or Mars.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
summary: NASA describes SANS as its leading spaceflight health risk: a group of eye and brain changes. In weightlessness, blood and cerebrospinal fluid shift toward the head, which can swell the optic nerve, fold the retina, flatten the back of the eye and swell the brain. About 70 percent of ISS astronauts show some swelling at the back of the eye, ranging from mild to clinically significant; long-term outcomes are unknown and risk grows with mission length. NASA studies nutritional supplements, mechanical ways to counter the fluid shift, and head-down tilt bed rest on Earth. ASTRA has no eye measurement; vision changes can only be self-reported.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Spaceflight-induced bone changes
summary: In microgravity, weight-bearing bones such as the spine and hips carry less load and lose density. On four- to six-month missions bones lose about 1 to 1.5 percent of their density per month, and researchers are still studying whether that rate continues on longer flights. This raises the risk of fractures and early bone weakening. Countermeasures include resistive exercise and bone scans before and after flight, and NASA has studied drug countermeasures. ASTRA does not measure bone; daily exercise is shown only as countermeasure context.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Altered immune system responses in spaceflight
section: Risk of altered immune system responses
summary: Spaceflight stressors such as radiation, microgravity and poor sleep can change how the immune system behaves. This may trigger allergic reactions or reactivate dormant viruses; some ISS crew have reported cold sores, rashes, unusual allergies and infections. Researchers track immune changes with blood, saliva and urine samples, including samples collected in flight. In ASTRA, skin rash and cold or flu symptoms can be self-reported; no immune marker is measured.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Altered sensorimotor and vestibular function
section: Risk of altered sensorimotor and vestibular function
summary: Changes in gravity, including moving between gravity levels, can cause motion sickness and make it harder to stay oriented. Most astronauts experience motion sickness during spaceflight, and it can affect tasks, vehicle operation and spacewalks. NASA studies how disoriented crews are right after landing, tests medications and orientation aids, and evaluates head-movement and recovery techniques in bed rest studies. ASTRA lets crew self-report nausea and dizziness; it has no balance sensor.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Cardiovascular adaptations in spaceflight
summary: Low gravity and other spaceflight stressors change the heart and blood vessels. This can lead to blood clots, irregular heartbeats, cardiovascular disease, and low blood pressure that raises fainting risk at landing. Crews counter it with regular exercise, healthy diets, lower-body compression garments and fluid loading before landing, and future Mars crews will train for cardiovascular emergencies. The risk grows on longer missions. ASTRA tracks synthetic heart rate, HRV and oxygen saturation against each person's own baseline; it does not diagnose heart disease.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Behavioral conditions and psychiatric disorders
section: Risk of behavioral conditions and psychiatric disorders
summary: Long isolation and confinement can raise the risk of behavioral problems such as anxiety and depression, which may disrupt sleep, morale and decision-making, especially when communication with Earth is delayed. NASA encourages crews to keep journals; research suggests growing fresh vegetables may help, spacecraft windows reduce monotony, and privacy is a priority. NASA tests strategies in Earth-based isolation analogs such as HERA. ASTRA offers a private mood and stress self-report, never a psychiatric score.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Inadequate sleep and irregular schedules
section: Risk from inadequate sleep and irregular schedules
summary: Sleep loss, disrupted body clocks and heavy workloads can reduce performance and harm health. Causes include work overload, irregular light-dark cycles and the space station's 16 sunrises and sunsets each day. Countermeasures include LED lighting that mimics Earth's day-night cycle and scheduled time for relaxation and self-care; researchers study how light and caffeine affect crew body clocks and sleep quality. ASTRA shows completed sleep sessions, fatigue and reaction time against each person's baseline.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Inadequate teamwork
summary: Weak cooperation, coordination, communication or social adjustment can lower crew performance and behavioral health. Mars missions intensify the causes: signal delays, long isolation, no resupply and living space much smaller than the ISS, which make conflicts harder to resolve. Astronauts practise team skills before flight and receive in-mission support, and NASA studies crew dynamics in Earth analogs that cannot fully recreate weightlessness. ASTRA's private self-report includes tension with crewmates.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Radiation-induced cancers and other radiation effects
summary: Astronauts receive more radiation in space than on the ground, which can lead to certain cancers and may raise the risk of degenerative conditions of the heart, blood vessels and eyes; exposure may also affect the brain and cognitive performance. Earth's magnetosphere shields the planet, but Moon and Mars missions travel beyond that protection. NASA is developing shielding, countermeasure medicines, health surveillance and radiation instruments on the ISS. ASTRA shows only a synthetic cabin dose rate with an illustrative review level; total mission dose is not tracked.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Reduced cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness
section: Risk of reduced cardiorespiratory and musculoskeletal fitness
summary: Living in microgravity weakens muscles, bones, heart and lungs, raising injury and fall risk when crews move to the Moon, Mars or back to Earth. Average strength and aerobic fitness losses are about 10 to 12 percent of pre-mission levels, and 12 to 38 percent of ISS crew members lose more than 20 percent. ISS astronauts exercise about 1.5 hours a day, and researchers are refining exercise devices and routines for smaller future spacecraft. ASTRA tracks daily exercise minutes as countermeasure context.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Host-microorganism interactions
summary: Spaceflight appears to change the communities of microbes on crew skin and in the gut, and some microbes seem more disease-causing in orbit; it is not yet clear whether the main risk comes from those shifts or from altered immune function. Crews can still get sick despite precautions such as limiting large-group contact in the two weeks before launch. Researchers test disinfectants and other countermeasures, and astronauts collect body and station-surface swabs. ASTRA does not monitor microbes.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Inadequate food and nutrition
section: Risk of inadequate food and nutrition
summary: Inadequate food and nutrition can reduce performance and cause illness. Space meals must be acceptable, safe, nutritious, long-lasting and easy to prepare, with enough variety to avoid menu fatigue. Moon and Mars missions make this harder because food must last longer, fit tight mass and volume limits and arrive without resupply. NASA is reducing sodium, adding foods and designing a deep-space food system. ASTRA does not track nutrition.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Hypoxia on exploration missions
summary: Mild hypoxia means tissue oxygen falls below normal. On deep-space missions it can come from keeping the cabin at a constantly reduced pressure, which supports frequent spacewalks. Untreated, it can cause confusion, headaches, vision problems and trouble sleeping. NASA is researching oxygen and pressure protocols, suit pressure options and health monitoring. ASTRA tracks synthetic oxygen saturation (SpO2) against each person's baseline; it is not a hypoxia diagnosis.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA risk page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Distance, gravity and closed environments: hazard details
section: Distance from Earth; gravity fields; hostile and closed environments
summary: Mars is on average about 140 million miles from Earth, and a Mars mission could last about three years, compared with a three-day trip to the Moon, so crews must plan for self-sufficiency. Mars gravity is about three-eighths of Earth's, and crews could live in it for up to two years; muscles, bones, the inner ear and organs must adjust to each gravity change, including the return to Earth. Inside a closed spacecraft, temperature, pressure, lighting, noise and microbes all matter, and NASA tracks microbial communities and immune responses. The hazards interact and can amplify one another.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Ongoing research on Artemis II: ARCHeR, Immune Biomarkers, Standard Measures
summary: For the Artemis II deep-space mission, NASA's ARCHeR study monitors crew well-being, activity and sleep, including a wrist-worn actigraphy device that records motion, sleep patterns and light exposure. The Immune Biomarkers study analyses blood and saliva samples to see how deep space affects immunity, and Artemis II Standard Measures collects a consistent set of crew health information for a research data bank. These studies inspire ASTRA's sleep, activity and self-report features; ASTRA uses synthetic data, not study data.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Ongoing research on the ISS: SANS, exercise, blood flow and landing studies
summary: ISS studies include B-Complex (whether a daily B-vitamin supplement can reduce eye and brain changes), Brain Fluid Pressure and Spinal Fluid Biomarkers (links between fluid pressure and SANS), and Thigh Cuff (whether tight thigh cuffs keep fluid in the legs). CIPHER studies many body systems at once, Standard Measures collects consistent physiological and psychological data, Zero T2 tests exercise without a treadmill, Venous Haemostasis examines blood flow and clotting, and other studies cover manual piloting after gravity transitions and crew comfort during re-entry.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of the public NASA page; no NASA endorsement.

title: Monitoring neutron radiation: the Canadian Active Neutron Spectrometer (CANS)
summary: The Canadian Space Agency awarded 5.5 million dollars to Bubble Technology Industries to develop CANS, a compact instrument that measures neutron radiation continuously and autonomously. Neutrons make up about 30 percent of the total radiation on the ISS and can cause serious biological damage. CANS follows earlier Canadian radiation experiments (MOSFET, EVARM, Radi-N and Radi-N2) and bubble detectors. ASTRA does not track neutron dose; this is a candidate future indicator.
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of a public Government of Canada page; no endorsement.

title: Why science experiments are done in space
summary: Space research prepares crews for longer Moon and Mars missions with more weightlessness, more radiation, longer isolation, communication delays and less access to Earth for supplies and emergency care. Weightlessness causes changes that resemble accelerated ageing and inactivity, so about six months of astronaut data can inform care on Earth for bones (osteoporosis), heart and blood vessels, balance problems in older adults, and metabolism (type 2 diabetes).
license_notes: Project-authored short paraphrase of a public Government of Canada page; no endorsement.
